hero.headline: Daughter files wrongful death suit after mother killed in Florida Turnpike crash in St. Lucie County
hero.teaser: Angeline Dowdian has filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother and two others were killed when their minivan became wedged under a semi-truck on August 12, 2025 in St. Lucie County.
hero.body:
On August 12, 2025, three people died in St. Lucie County when their minivan was crushed beneath a semi-truck. The victims were Herby Dufresne, 30, Rodrigue Dor, 54, and Faniola Joseph, 37, who had traveled to Florida from Indiana to purchase inventory for her shop. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly made an illegal U-turn in a marked no-turn zone, causing the collision. Now Joseph's daughter, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, his employer White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson. The lawsuit claims negligence and unsafe practices contributed to the tragedy. Singh also faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida.

Angeline, represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer, describes the profound impact of her mother's death. Living abroad at the time of the crash, Angeline had not seen her mother in person for six years, though they spoke daily through video calls. The day of the accident, her mother left a voice message that Angeline says she listens to every morning. "She sent me a voice message. She said, 'Angeline, where are you?' This is the first message I go to every morning," Angeline said through tears. Her mother was both parents to her since her father rejected her at birth. Visa restrictions have prevented Angeline from visiting her mother's grave. Joseph had hoped to see her daughter become a nurse and would have turned 38 on May 26, 2026.

The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly continued business with White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations. Bello argues this was not an accident but a predictable outcome. A transportation expert has characterized White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." The case is strengthened by a May 14 Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, the same broker named in this lawsuit, which clarified that federal law does not protect freight brokers from state negligence claims when they place unsafe drivers on roads. According to Justice Brett Kavanaugh's concurring opinion, "Some carriers are known to be less safe, and some truck drivers are known to be unfit." Bello maintains that brokers have a responsibility to review publicly available safety records before hiring drivers.

White Hawk Carriers has closed, though Bello warns the company may reopen under a different name, a common industry practice. Bello, a former homicide prosecutor, is helping Angeline navigate both civil and criminal proceedings under Marsy's Law, which provides victims' families with rights to be informed and heard. Angeline acknowledges that no legal victory will reverse her loss but hopes the lawsuit prevents other families from suffering similar tragedy. "I don't want nobody suffer like me," she said.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after shooting in Fort Pierce leaves another teen critically wounded
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce left another 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended the three suspects. One was caught by a sheriff's office K9, and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss from property tax amendment on November ballot
cards.teaser: Indian River County leaders warned Friday that a property tax amendment on the November ballot could cost the county around $50 million by 2028.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Vice Chair Laura Moss convened the meeting, criticizing the state for dictating local funding decisions. "They've declared war on local government," Moss said. The county operates on a budget of approximately $597 million and predicts it could lose around $50 million in funding by 2028.

Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, characterized the amendment as a tax shift rather than a tax cut. He warned that filling the $50 million shortfall without reducing law enforcement and first responder services would be impossible. The shift could increase costs on non-homesteaded and commercial properties, as well as government service fees like impact fees and utility fees. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said fire rescue could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, since about 79.1 percent of fire rescue funding comes from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs.

cards.headline: Florida GOP debate standoff intensifies as DeSantis backs calls for gubernatorial candidates to face off
cards.teaser: A dispute over debates has erupted in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary, with Gov.
cards.body:
A dispute over Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary has intensified into a debate about debates, with Gov. Ron DeSantis joining several candidates in calling for a public showdown. The Republican Party of Florida announced Friday that its June 27 Sunshine State Showdown in Hollywood will not include a full debate between candidates seeking to succeed the term-limited DeSantis. The party set three qualification benchmarks: at least 10% polling support, more than $10 million raised, and more than 10,000 donors. Only U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican front-runner, cleared all three thresholds. A party poll conducted June 9 and 10 found Donalds leading with 38.8% support, followed by Jay Collins at 7.6%, businessman James Fishback at 4.1%, and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2.2%. Nearly 43% of likely Republican primary voters remained undecided.

DeSantis criticized both the qualification criteria and party control of the process, saying he would not have qualified under the standards when he ran in 2018. He argued debates should be arranged by candidates and media organizations, warning that limiting participation could alienate voters and weaken the Republican brand. Renner and Collins called for a debate before the Aug. 18 primary. Donalds dismissed the pressure, with his campaign communications director stating there are "no participation trophies in politics." On Friday, the Florida GOP rescinded Fishback's invitation to official primary activities after he announced a competing July 15 debate, citing violation of party rules.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter and apprehended the three suspects. One was caught by a sheriff's office K9 and another was found hiding in a recycling container. cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss under property tax amendment
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose approximately $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday morning at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to the Tax Payers Association, the county's $597 million budget could lose approximately $50 million in funding by 2028. Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, criticized the measure as state interference in local governance. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called it an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy.

Fire rescue services face particularly significant cuts. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said the department could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Lunceford warned the amendment represents a tax shift rather than a tax cut, likely requiring the county to raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties and increase costs for services such as impact fees and utility fees to compensate for lost revenue.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen from Boys & Girls Clubs wins Southeast Youth of the Year, heads to national competition
hero.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian of St. Lucie High School, became the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to win Southeast Region Youth of the Year. He will compete nationally in New York City on October 1.
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz has become the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to earn the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. The St. Lucie High School valedictorian will now compete for the national title at the Youth of the Year competition in New York City on October 1. His achievement marks a significant milestone for the local organization and represents years of dedication to academics, personal values, and community leadership.

Enrique's path to this recognition began eight years ago when he arrived in Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic without speaking English. Rather than viewing this challenge as a barrier, he used the support from his school and the Boys & Girls Club to build his skills and confidence. Today, he holds the titles of both county and Florida Youth of the Year. This fall, he will begin his college career at the University of Florida. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old," Enrique said after receiving the award. "It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity."

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, highlighted Enrique's character and growth. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination." Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime judge for the Youth of the Year program, reinforced this assessment. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community."

The Youth of the Year program represents the highest honor given by Boys & Girls Clubs of America to recognize exceptional teenagers who demonstrate leadership and positive change in their communities. Enrique's parents expressed their pride in their son's accomplishments. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said. As Enrique prepares to represent the Southeast Region on the national stage, his journey continues to inspire young people throughout the community.

cards.headline: Delray Beach memorial for Pulse victims stalls as new state law threatens local government funding
cards.teaser: A proposed Pride memorial honoring 49 victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre has been delayed by Senate Bill 1134, which could ban local governments from supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.
cards.body:
Friday, June 12 marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. In Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted intersection once honored the victims until the Florida Department of Transportation sandblasted it away in August 2025 due to statewide pressure to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. The state also removed the rainbow crosswalk outside Pulse in Orlando, while Boynton Beach preemptively removed theirs and West Palm Beach replaced a Pride crosswalk in Northwood with a rainbow corner in a nearby park.

The Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee formed to design a replacement, proposing a rainbow pyramid monument etched with the meaning behind each color and illuminated at night. The committee suggested placing it at Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the mural once stood. However, Commissioner Juli Casal cited Senate Bill 1134, awaiting the governor's decision, as a legal barrier. The bill, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and could jeopardize state funding if municipalities use city property or dollars for such projects. Casal said the project could accelerate with private funding and private property.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit against trucking company and freight broker
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother Faniola Joseph and two others were killed when their minivan became wedged under a semi-truck in St. Lucie County on August 12, 2025.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, a minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck in St. Lucie County after the truck's driver, Harjinder Singh, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. The crash killed three people: Faniola Joseph, 37, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54. Joseph had traveled from Indiana to purchase goods for her shop. Her daughter, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, his employer White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices.

Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson knowingly contracted with White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Bello cited a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. The same broker was involved in that case. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has shut down.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with murder of 76-year-old grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, admitted to killing his grandmother Patricia Ann DiBella, who was found dead inside her home at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach in February.
cards.body:
A 29-year-old Vero Beach man is accused of killing his 76-year-old grandmother, who was found dead inside her home in February. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that Nicholas Leonard Ivey now faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of Patricia Ann DiBella. Investigators said Ivey admitted to killing DiBella, who had opened her home to him at her residence at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. The following day, a welfare check was requested by family members, which led deputies to the scene, where Ivey was taken into custody. Since February, Ivey has been held on other related charges. The sheriff's office formally charged him with murder on June 3. Ivey is being held at the Indian River County Jail without bond.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement that he is proud of the work the investigations team did to bring justice to Patricia DiBella and her family. "No one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. I encourage anyone experiencing domestic violence to contact law enforcement," Flowers said. The sheriff's office reminded the community that domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone. Anyone in danger can call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce marks 25th anniversary
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium in Fort Pierce offers rare close-up encounters with Florida coastal marine life and is celebrating its 25th anniversary later this year.
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal underwater habitats along Fort Pierce's waterfront. Manager Bill Hoffman explains that the facility's approach of displaying fully live, complex ecosystem models began in 1980 under the Smithsonian, distinguishing it from most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman said, pointing out that the facility houses more species than many larger exhibits. Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the aquarium operates year-round and welcomes the public to experience marine life up close.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, which recreates one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems in vivid detail. Beyond the coral reef, visitors encounter live representations of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. Each display demonstrates how organisms interact and depend on one another within their habitats. The collection includes unexpected residents, such as the facility's four-inch barracuda, showing the diversity of marine life in Florida's waters.

A popular attraction for many guests is the touch tank, where visitors handle unusual marine species under the watchful eye of trained staff members. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran notes that guests often encounter animals they have never seen before. This hands-on experience creates memorable connections between visitors and the marine world. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit partners with the Smithsonian Marine Station to raise public awareness about ocean threats while promoting conservation efforts. Hoffman stresses that maintaining healthy ecosystems requires understanding the critical role of countless small organisms, a lesson reinforced through the facility's live displays.

As the exhibit celebrates its 25th anniversary this year, upcoming programming will highlight the facility's mission and history. With growing concerns about ocean health, exhibits like this one in Fort Pierce provide valuable educational opportunities for visitors of all ages. They create connections between people and the fragile beauty and importance of Florida's marine ecosystems. For more information about hours, exhibits, and programming, visitors can check sms.si.edu and the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels.

cards.headline: Hundreds of fish die in Port St. Lucie community after city algae treatment
cards.teaser: Dead fish floated on the water at the Sawgrass Lakes community in Port St. Lucie on Thursday after the city hired a vendor to treat the water for algae earlier in the week.
cards.body:
Dead fish floated on the water at Sawgrass Lakes in Port St. Lucie on Thursday morning after the city treated the water for algae earlier in the week. Neighbors shared videos of the die-off they discovered in their backyards. "There were hundreds and hundreds of fish here, and thousands of those little ones just gulping the air," said neighbor Jim Herbert. The city hired SOLitude on Tuesday and Wednesday to treat the water for algae. Experts told WPTV that with high heat and algae treatment, the water can become uninhabitable for aquatic life. On Thursday, crews removed the dead fish and tested oxygen levels in the water. Herbert said this was at least the second fish die-off since he has lived in the neighborhood.

Scott Samples with the city of Port St. Lucie said the city has been working with neighbors and other cities and counties to find solutions. "We're hoping that there might be a couple of options soon," Samples said. "But those are sort of dependent on a couple of things, and so we have not been able to do that yet." Neighbor Jerry Cook said he does not think the issue is an overnight or couple-month fix, but a few years fix. Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, said the city should look at more natural solutions, including planting aquatic vegetation, reducing fertilizer use, and removing sediment that fuels algae growth. "We're going to end up in a cycle that we can't break unless we go back to square one and start with a natural remediation," Moir said.

cards.headline: Wellington posts highest rental costs in Palm Beach County at nearly $2,850 for one-bedroom
cards.teaser: Wellington residents face the highest rental costs in Palm Beach County, with Fair Market Rent reaching nearly $2,850 for a one-bedroom apartment, according to new 2026 data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
cards.body:
Wellington residents face the highest rental costs in Palm Beach County, with Fair Market Rent reaching nearly $2,850 for a one-bedroom apartment, according to 2026 data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. The ZIP code 33449 in Wellington posted the county's highest Fair Market Rent rates, with four-bedroom homes exceeding $5,080 monthly. In contrast, Belle Glade offers the county's most affordable rental market at $890 for comparable housing. Luis Rivera, who lives in Section 8 housing in Palm Beach County, said the market conditions are difficult. "You have to budget, there's no way out of it," Rivera said, noting he was seeing rental prices over two to three thousand dollars in neighborhoods that weren't even reasonable.

Real estate broker Talbot Sutter, president of Sutter and Nugent Real Estate, attributes Wellington's high costs to quality amenities and location advantages. "A lot of it has to do with school districts, especially Wellington. They have like top A-rated schools, lifestyle, they have so many aspects from equestrian to outdoor activities," Sutter said. Sutter works with high-end clients, often executives from New York City, who rent luxury properties before purchasing. HUD's Fair Market Rent data reveals substantial price variations across neighboring counties for one-bedroom apartments: Okeechobee County at $1,032, Indian River County at $1,222, and St. Lucie and Martin areas at $1,467.

cards.headline: Fresh produce prices force Treasure Coast shoppers to change grocery habits
cards.teaser: Fresh fruit and vegetable prices climbed more than 6% over the past year, according to Thursday's federal inflation report, forcing Palm Beach County shoppers to adapt their purchasing strategies.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County shoppers are changing their grocery habits as fresh fruit and vegetable prices climbed more than 6% over the past year, according to Thursday's federal inflation report and a new study from financial services company Advance America. One in three American families now purchase fewer fresh fruits and vegetables due to rising costs, while 20% have switched to frozen alternatives. One Palm Beach County shopper explained the switch to frozen produce, saying "the quality is still the same, as you can get organic and all those things for quite the same price that you would find fresh." Another resident described expanding his shopping routine to multiple locations, including Don Victor's in Lake Worth, which he called "a great place to get vegetables," noting his shopping day now consists of two or three stops.

Not all consumers are dramatically changing their purchasing patterns. One shopper said rising prices are manageable for her situation, explaining "I'm shopping only for one most of the time" and still buying fresh produce in moderate quantities. The Advance America study found Florida residents now spend over $28 more monthly on groceries compared to previous periods. Federal data shows overall grocery prices increased 2.7% year-over-year through May, with fresh produce leading the increases at more than 6%. The shift toward frozen and canned alternatives could have lasting effects on local grocery retailers and consumer nutrition habits.

cards.headline: Delray Beach struggles to honor Pulse victims 10 years after massacre amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: Friday marks 10 years since the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives. Delray Beach faces mounting obstacles in replacing a memorial that was removed by the state.
cards.body:
Just blocks from downtown Delray Beach, a rainbow-painted intersection once honored the victims of the Pulse nightclub massacre in Orlando, where 49 people lost their lives 10 years ago on June 12. Local residents funded and created the Pride mural themselves, but it now stands as faded bricks. In August 2025, Delray Beach leaders argued the mural sat on city property and pushed back against state pressure to remove it. Within weeks, the Florida Department of Transportation sandblasted away the vibrant rainbow to comply with a statewide push to regulate road markings and remove political and ideological messaging. The state also removed the rainbow crosswalk outside Pulse in Orlando, while Boynton Beach preemptively took theirs down and West Palm Beach removed a Pride crosswalk in Northwood before later replacing it with a rainbow corner in a nearby park.

Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee, which by March designed a rainbow pyramid monument etched with color meanings and illuminated at night. Dunayer proposed placing it at Old School Square, near the Eagle Scout monument and steps from where the Pride mural once stood. Commissioner Juli Casal cited Senate Bill 1134, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House, as a barrier. The bill, awaiting the governor's decision, would ban local governments from funding diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and could put state funding at risk. Casal stated that private funding and private property could allow the memorial to be completed immediately.

cards.headline: Daughter of St. Lucie County crash victim files wrongful death lawsuit
cards.teaser: On August 12, 2025, three people were killed when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck on the Florida Turnpike in St. Lucie County. Now the daughter of one victim has filed a wrongful death lawsuit.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, were killed in St. Lucie County when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, who worked for White Hawk Carriers, allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. Joseph's 22-year-old daughter, Angeline Dowdian, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. Attorney Dax Bello of Stuart Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane argues the crash was not an accident but "a predictable end that came at the cost of three lives." The lawsuit alleges C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. The case is supported by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. She missed a call from her mother on the day of the crash and receives a voice message from her each morning asking, "Angeline, where are you?" Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down, though Bello warns the company may reopen under another name.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce showcases Florida's coastal habitats
hero.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium is inviting visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats with rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district.
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal waters through live, complex ecosystem displays. The facility's approach to education has been rooted in this philosophy since 1980, setting it apart from typical public aquariums. Manager Bill Hoffman emphasized the facility's significance to WPTV, saying the team views itself as the area's best kept secret and hopes to change that perception. He noted that despite its size, the aquarium houses more species than many larger facilities across the region.

The centerpiece of the exhibit is the Atlantic coral reef tank, a large display that recreates one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems. Beyond the reef, visitors encounter living models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. These displays reveal how different organisms depend on one another, with examples including a surprisingly small four-inch barracuda. The exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran highlighted the touch tank as a visitor favorite, where guests can handle unusual marine species with staff supervision and encounter animals they may never have encountered before.

The exhibit operates through a partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, focusing on educating the public about ocean threats while promoting conservation efforts. Hoffman stressed that stable marine ecosystems rely on countless small organisms, a concept reinforced through the facility's live displays. The aquarium is marking its 25th anniversary celebration later this year with upcoming programming tied to this milestone.

Located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce, the facility welcomes visitors throughout the year. More information is available through sms.si.edu and the Smithsonian Marine Station's social media channels. As ocean health concerns grow, exhibits like this one provide valuable educational opportunities for visitors of all ages, connecting them to the fragile ecosystems and marine life that define Florida's coastal waters.

cards.headline: Curaçao soccer team trains in Boca Raton before Sunday's historic World Cup debut, draws Port St. Lucie fans
cards.teaser: Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday to witness Curaçao's national team prepare for its first-ever World.
cards.body:
Hundreds of soccer fans filled Florida Atlantic University stadium in Boca Raton on Thursday, waving jerseys and flags to witness Curaçao prepare for its first-ever World Cup appearance. The team, known as the "Blue Wave," held a training session that drew enthusiastic supporters eager to catch a glimpse of their favorite players ahead of the historic debut. Goalkeeper Eloy Room told WPTV the outpouring of support has fueled the team's excitement. "Really joyful to see that so many people showed up today — it gives us energy. We're really excited to start the World Cup," Room said. Midfielder Tahitch Chong said the moment carries enormous meaning for the entire island. "I think it's amazing to see. I don't think the people back home are going to believe the crowd we had here," Chong said.

Curaçao, an island nation with a population of just over 150,000 people, is the smallest nation to qualify for the tournament and went undefeated in all 10 of its 2026 World Cup qualifying matches. Fans traveled from across South Florida for the event, with some Curaçao natives making the drive from as far as Port St. Lucie. Marionella Barzeycoggins, originally from Curaçao, said she made sure her whole family attended. "I found out they're gonna be in Boca and they have a training event. And I'm like, oh my God, I have to RSVP so we are here," Barzeycoggins said. Curaçao faces Germany this Sunday in Houston, Texas.

cards.headline: Lake Worth woman born without right hand pulled over by Palm Beach County deputy for allegedly holding phone
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. Thomas was born without a right hand.
cards.body:
A Palm Beach County deputy pulled over Lake Worth resident Katie Thomas for allegedly holding her phone in her right hand while driving. The traffic stop went viral on social media, generating 110 million views, after body camera footage revealed an immediate problem: Thomas was born without a right hand. During the stop, the deputy told Thomas, "You drove past me, holding the phone with your right hand, manipulating that phone." Thomas responded by raising her arm to show her stump. When the deputy pressed further, asking if she had her phone in her hand, Thomas repeatedly replied "Hand to God" to deny the claim.

Thomas, an adaptive athlete who has spent her life raising awareness for the limb-difference community, said being accused of something she did not have a limb to be accused of was one of the most captivating aspects of the incident. The citation was dropped for lack of evidence. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said an agency review of the case is underway. Thomas said she harbors no ill will toward the sheriff's office and has started selling "Hand to God" merchandise on her Instagram, with proceeds benefiting Shriners Children's Hospital. She said she has no plans to sue.

hero.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at Fort Pierce aquarium offers close encounters with Florida coastal life
hero.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's underwater world at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman explains that the facility's approach to displaying live, complex ecosystem models has been a cornerstone since 1980 under Smithsonian direction, distinguishing it from typical public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV. He points out that the aquarium houses more species than many larger facilities across the country.

The centerpiece is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a large tank that recreates one of Florida's most important coastal ecosystems. Beyond the reef display, visitors encounter live representations of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities. These exhibits demonstrate the complex connections between different organisms in each habitat. Even smaller creatures get attention here, including a barracuda that measures just four inches, illustrating how stable ecosystems depend on countless small organisms throughout the food chain.

The touch tank ranks among the most popular attractions at the facility. Exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran notes that this hands-on experience allows guests to handle marine species they've likely never encountered before, all under the guidance of trained staff members. The aquarium is planning special programming around its 25th anniversary celebration scheduled for later this year.

Working in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, the exhibit aims to educate the public about ocean threats while inspiring conservation efforts. Hoffman stresses that understanding how small organisms support entire ecosystems is central to the facility's mission. The aquarium operates year-round and welcomes visitors to discover why ocean health matters. Those interested in learning more can visit sms.si.edu or follow the Smithsonian Marine Station on social media channels.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Public Library offers free STREAM summer programs with daily lunches for kids and teens
cards.teaser: The Delray Beach Public Library at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue is launching free Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math programs for all Florida residents this summer.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Public Library is offering free STREAM summer programs—Science, Technology, Reading, Art, Engineering and Math—to kids and teens. Kae Jonsons, director of development and community relations, told WPTV the library has served the community since 1913, when 30 women from the Ladies Improvement Society each donated a book to start the collection. Today, the 36,000-square-foot facility at Atlantic Avenue and Swinton Avenue welcomes more than 193,000 visitors annually. Natalie Baron, young adult librarian, leads sessions like ColorSpace: Artistic Excavations, where teens explore art history from cave paintings to ancient pottery. Teens can also join lab-based activities including collaborative 3D puzzle builds and pick up themed book boxes.

Mandy Fulop, head of the children's department, is launching the STREAM Into Summer Literacy Program, encouraging readers to set goals with librarians, track progress, and take home an Unearth a Story bag with a free STREAM book and activities. In partnership with the School District of Palm Beach County, the library serves free lunch daily from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and snacks from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. to youth up to 18. Family Nights on select Tuesdays invite children 5 and up to explore STREAM topics together. Saturday Science Discovery programs for ages 9 to 12 feature hands-on archaeology activities. Upcoming Thursday guests include Malachi Fenn from the Florida Public Archaeology Network on June 11, Sea Turtle Adventures beach cleanup on June 25, American Shark Conservancy's SharkSmarts on July 2, and FPAN Beyond Artifacts on July 16. Registration is available at delraylibrary.org.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores house adoptable cats during Palm City shelter renovations
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two Stuart thrift stores to house cats while construction continues on adoption, customer service, and intake areas at its Palm City shelter.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is housing adoptable cats at its two thrift stores while undergoing major renovations at its Palm City shelter. The nonprofit began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily relocating many of its cats to the store locations. Spokesperson Sarah Fisher explained that the stores have become essential during this period. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," she said Thursday.

Senior Manager Kelly Ellis noted that shoppers can now browse unique items for sale while also viewing adoptable cats at both thrift stores. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis said, welcoming donations of gently used goods. The organization is also seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st Street in Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

hero.headline: Florida economic outlook downgraded as tourism growth slows amid global instability
hero.teaser: Florida TaxWatch projects the state will add 2.3 million residents by 2035 but has lowered expectations for tourism, unemployment, and income growth compared to previous forecasts.
hero.body:
Florida TaxWatch released its latest economic outlook projecting that Florida will add roughly 2.3 million residents between 2026 and 2035 and continue to outperform the national economy in terms of growth. However, compared to its previous forecast, TaxWatch has downgraded expectations for several key indicators, citing global instability, rising energy costs, and uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Population growth is still expected to climb from 23.8 million in 2026 to just over 26 million by 2035, with daily net migration gradually slowing from about 895 people a day to 689. Despite economic headwinds, Florida continues to attract new residents thanks to its business climate, lack of a personal income tax, and favorable weather.

The labor market presents a less favorable picture. While total employment is expected to grow from 10.1 million workers to 11.3 million over the next decade, TaxWatch now expects unemployment to rise higher and remain elevated longer than previously forecast. The statewide unemployment rate is projected to peak at 4.8% in 2027, then gradually settle near 4.2% in the early 2030s. Income growth expectations have also been lowered. Per-capita personal income is still projected to rise from roughly $88,000 in 2026 to more than $126,000 by 2035, but overall income projections declined by an average of 10.3% compared to the prior forecast.

Tourism represents the biggest downgrade in the outlook. TaxWatch's growth expectations for visitor numbers have fallen by an average of 45.3% since the previous report, making tourism the sector most affected by current headwinds. Visitor counts are still expected to increase each year, but the pace of growth is projected to slow dramatically, bottoming out at just 0.8% in 2027. Despite this slowdown, Florida's broader economic output is expected to perform relatively well. Real GDP growth will slow from 2.5% in 2026 to 1.9% in 2027 before rebounding above 3% for much of the following decade.

The primary uncertainty shaping TaxWatch's outlook centers on Middle Eastern geopolitics. The watchdog group repeatedly points to uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil passes, as the single biggest factor influencing its projections. If energy markets stabilize, the group suggests many of its more pessimistic assumptions could ease, potentially allowing Florida to avoid a rougher economic ride. The overall message from the report frames Florida as resilient but not immune to broader economic pressures.

cards.headline: Florida GOP debate standoff intensifies as DeSantis backs calls for gubernatorial candidates to face off
cards.teaser: A dispute over debates has erupted in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary, with Gov.
cards.body:
A dispute over Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary has intensified into a debate about debates, with Gov. Ron DeSantis joining several candidates in calling for a public showdown. The Republican Party of Florida announced Friday that its June 27 Sunshine State Showdown in Hollywood will not include a full debate between candidates seeking to succeed the term-limited DeSantis. The party set three qualification benchmarks: at least 10% polling support, more than $10 million raised, and more than 10,000 donors. Only U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, the Republican front-runner, cleared all three thresholds. A party poll conducted June 9 and 10 found Donalds leading with 38.8% support, followed by Jay Collins at 7.6%, businessman James Fishback at 4.1%, and former Florida House Speaker Paul Renner at 2.2%. Nearly 43% of likely Republican primary voters remained undecided.

DeSantis criticized both the qualification criteria and party control of the process, saying he would not have qualified under the standards when he ran in 2018. He argued debates should be arranged by candidates and media organizations, warning that limiting participation could alienate voters and weaken the Republican brand. Renner and Collins called for a debate before the Aug. 18 primary. Donalds dismissed the pressure, with his campaign communications director stating there are "no participation trophies in politics." On Friday, the Florida GOP rescinded Fishback's invitation to official primary activities after he announced a competing July 15 debate, citing violation of party rules.

cards.headline: DeSantis grants Florida state workers two extra days off for America 250 celebration
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Friday that state offices will close on July 2 and July 6, giving Florida's 100,000 state employees additional time to celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary.
cards.body:
Ron DeSantis is giving employees of the state of Florida two additional days off next month as the nation celebrates America 250. State offices will be closed on Thursday, July 2, 2026, and Monday, July 6, 2026, DeSantis announced Friday. This will give Florida's 100,000 state employees more time to celebrate the nation's independence. "America's 250th anniversary is a historic milestone and an opportunity to reflect on the courage, sacrifice, and enduring principles that established the United States as the freest and most prosperous nation in the world," DeSantis said.

Florida has been leaning into the historic America 250 occasion. "As Florida leads the nation's semiquincentennial celebration, I am pleased to provide state employees additional time to celebrate our country's founding, participate in America 250 events, and spend time with family and friends honoring the blessings of liberty that generations of Americans have fought to preserve," DeSantis added. DeSantis has said Florida was the 14th colony at various points and has framed the celebration as a way to remind Floridians of American history and the Sunshine State's unique role from the beginning of the Republic. As part of the celebration, DeSantis has made it a focus to procure statues of historic figures, which have been put on display throughout the state.

cards.headline: Florida Supreme Court allows new congressional map to proceed for 2026 midterms
cards.teaser: The Florida Supreme Court denied a petition from voting rights groups seeking to block implementation of a new congressional map, clearing the way for it to be used in this year's elections.
cards.body:
The Florida Supreme Court denied a petition from voting rights groups seeking to block implementation of the state's new congressional map for the midterm elections. Equal Ground Protection Fund and other organizations argued that using the map this year could harm voters if it were later determined to be illegal. A Leon County circuit judge had already rejected a request for an injunction on the map, and the 1st District Court of Appeal declined to reverse that decision. In a 6-1 majority decision, the Supreme Court stated it would not intervene, saying "At this time, we do not have jurisdiction over that matter, and we do not simply assume that the 1st District's decision will provide an appropriate basis for this Court's review."

The new congressional districts will now be used for the 2026 elections. The map, approved by Gov. Ron DeSantis, has significantly altered several districts across Florida, including changes that reduced the number of Black-majority districts. DeSantis stated the changes were necessary to create a race-neutral map, anticipating that the Supreme Court would make it harder to use race as a factor in redistricting.

cards.headline: Eleven Republicans qualify for crowded race to succeed Byron Donalds in Congress
cards.teaser: Florida's 19th Congressional District will host the state's most crowded field of congressional candidates, with 11 Republicans competing in the primary to replace Rep. Byron Donalds.
cards.body:
With Byron Donalds running for Governor, Florida's 19th Congressional District will host the most crowded field of congressional candidates in the state. The Republican Primary field includes two former Congressmen who previously represented other states: Madison Cawthorn and Chris Collins. Major self-funders include Jim Oberweis, a dairy farm owner and former Illinois lawmaker, and Jim Schwartzel, president of Sun Broadcasting. Others with high profiles include author and health activist Catalina Lauf and former congressional staffer Ola Hawatmeh. Veteran Mike Pedersen also qualified, as did late entries Greg "Tex" Bukowski, a Sarasota County Charter Review Board member, and Linda Sawyer, a former researcher at the National Institutes of Health. January 6 insurrectionist John Strand also has a place on the GOP Primary ballot. Constitutionalist Seth Haskin also qualified shortly before the deadline, bringing the total to 11 Republicans running for the open seat.

On the Democratic side, Howard Sapp, a former state House candidate and air traffic controller, and Victor Arias, managing attorney of Arias Law Firm, made the ballot. Shortly before the deadline, Robert Neeld, who previously challenged former GOP Reps. Connie Mack IV and Rooney, also qualified for the Democratic Primary. Seth Haskin also qualified in the race without party affiliation and will face whoever wins the Democratic and Republican nominations in August. The winner of the Republican Primary will be a heavy favorite to win the Republican-heavy district. More than 69% of voters in the district voted for Republican Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election while just 34% backed Democrat Kamala Harris.

cards.headline: Ten candidates qualify for race to succeed Frederica Wilson in Congress
cards.teaser: Seven Democrats, one Republican, one independent, and one write-in candidate qualified for the race in Florida's 24th Congressional District, with several well-known candidates competing for the deeply blue seat.
cards.body:
A race to replace longtime Democratic U.S. Rep. Frederica Wilson in Florida's 24th Congressional District is set with 10 candidates after the qualifying deadline Friday. The contest features seven Democrats, one Republican, one person with no party affiliation, and a write-in candidate. CD 24, redrawn under a mid-decade redistricting plan drafted by Gov. Ron DeSantis' office, covers Miami Gardens in Miami-Dade and Hollywood, Miramar, and Pembroke Park in Broward County. The district is deeply blue, and the winner in November will almost assuredly be a Democrat.

State Sen. Shevrin Jones, Chair of the Miami-Dade County Democratic Party and a former in-line candidate for Senate Democratic Leader, is a favorite in the race. He pointed to legislation he passed, including the Dignity for Incarcerated Women Act, Blue Envelope Program, and Infectious Disease Elimination Program. Also prominent is Miami-Dade Commissioner Oliver Gilbert, a former Mayor of Miami Gardens and immediate past Chair of the County Commission, who reported $250,000 raised in just the first five days of his campaign. Other Democrats include former lawyer Kendrick Meek Jr., son and grandson of two former members of Congress; Miami-Dade Commissioner Jean Monestime; and doctor, lawyer, and repeat congressional candidate Rudolph "Rudy" Moise. Cultural leader Marshall Davis and civil rights lawyer Roderick Vereen also qualified. Republican candidate Te Mayonna Brown is a self-described real estate developer. NPA candidate Andy Daro is a sitting North Bay Village Commissioner. Patricia Gonzalez is a write-in candidate. The Primary Election is Aug. 18, followed by the General Election in November.

cards.headline: Debbie Wasserman Schultz becomes only white candidate in CD 20 Democratic Primary
cards.teaser: Four Black candidates qualified alongside Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz for the Democratic Primary in Florida's 20th Congressional District, a race shadowed by allegations of antisemitism and questions about representation.
cards.body:
Four Black candidates have qualified for the closely watched Democratic Primary in Florida's 20th Congressional District alongside Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the longest-serving Democrat in Florida's congressional delegation and the only White candidate in the race. Other candidates include Luther Campbell, a rapper who became a community leader; former U.S. Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick; former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness; and progressive activist Elijah Manley. Since the early 1990s, District 20 has had a Black-majority population, but a new map approved by Gov. Ron DeSantis changed that demographic composition. The Governor said the changes were needed to create a "race-neutral" map. People in the district have not had representation since Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in April to avoid a possible expulsion vote after an Ethics investigation found she broke House rules 25 times. She is also under federal investigation for allegedly directing over $5 million in federal disaster funds to her 2021 campaign. At least two polls show her trailing several other candidates.

Manley has raised the most money among those challenging Wasserman Schultz, while Holness lost the last Democratic Primary for this seat by just five votes. Campbell, the frontman for 2 Live Crew, is well known and can fund his own campaign. The Democratic Primary will probably decide the next representative, as about 68 percent voted for Harris for President. Wasserman Schultz has faced criticism for running in a seat traditionally represented by Black candidates. The race has also seen concerns about possible antisemitism, with Holness accused of questioning whether Jews were trying to win all the region's congressional seats, though he denies this. Campbell suggested in a social media video that U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz, also Jewish, worked with Wasserman Schultz to decide where each would run.

cards.teaser: University of Florida students have expressed support for Stuart Bell as their school's next president.
cards.body: University of Florida students have expressed support for Stuart Bell as their school's next president during the selection process. The university is currently searching for its next president to lead the institution.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen makes history as first Southeast Youth of the Year from St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz, the valedictorian at Lucie High School, has achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to earn the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. His accomplishment comes eight years after arriving in Port St. Lucie from the Dominican Republic without knowing English. Through support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he transformed himself into a leader and scholar. This fall, he will attend the University of Florida, but first he must travel to New York City on October 1 to compete for the national Youth of the Year title.

The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award recognizes outstanding teenagers in the Boys & Girls Clubs community who demonstrate academic excellence, strong values, and commitment to service leadership. Enrique has already been named Florida Youth of the Year, paving his way to the national stage. Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, praised Enrique's character and growth. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime judge for the award, also noted Enrique's exceptional qualities. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community," Leonard said.

Enrique reflects on his journey with gratitude and hope for others facing similar challenges. "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old. It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity," he shared. His parents expressed their own pride and appreciation for the support their son received. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said.

The Youth of the Year program represents the Boys & Girls Clubs of America's premier recognition of teenagers who serve as role models and change-makers in their communities. Enrique's rise from newcomer to valedictorian to regional award winner marks a significant moment for St. Lucie County. As he prepares for the national competition, his story continues to inspire young people throughout the region to pursue their own goals and overcome obstacles.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide in Fort Pierce shooting, victim in critical condition
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old was arrested and charged with attempted homicide after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. Another 16-year-old was found with gunshot wounds and remains in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old is facing an attempted homicide charge after a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Another juvenile was discovered laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One was caught by a sheriff's office K9, and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered. The 16-year-old victim was in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning. The 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.

cards.headline: Daughter of Florida Turnpike crash victim files wrongful death suit against freight broker, trucking company
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a wrongful death lawsuit after her mother Faniola Joseph and two others were killed when their minivan became wedged under a semi-truck in St. Lucie County on August 12, 2025.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, a minivan carrying Faniola Joseph, 37, Herby Dufresne, 30, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, became wedged underneath a semi-truck in St. Lucie County when the truck's driver allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. All three occupants were killed. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, worked for White Hawk Carriers. Joseph's daughter, Angeline Dowdian, 22, has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson. Angeline is represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer. The lawsuit alleges that C.H. Robinson, a multibillion-dollar freight broker, knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations in its record. Transportation expert James Lewis described White Hawk's violations as "very egregious." Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida.

Angeline lived in another country at the time of the crash and had not seen her mother in person in six years, though they spoke daily via video calls. On the crash day, she missed a call from her mother. Angeline described her mother as both parents to her since her father rejected her at birth. Visa restrictions have prevented her from visiting her mother's grave. The case is strengthened by a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit in Fort Pierce showcases Florida coastal habitats
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium offers rare close-up encounters with marine life at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. Hoffman told WPTV that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating the intricate relationships between organisms, including the aquarium's four-inch barracuda.

The exhibit's touch tank is another crowd favorite, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff guidance. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor charged with child neglect of five foster children
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce pastor faces child neglect charges involving five foster children in his care.
cards.body:
A pastor in Fort Pierce has been charged with child neglect of five foster children. The charges were filed Friday. No additional information about the specific allegations or the identity of the pastor was available in the initial report.

The case involves multiple foster children who were in the care of the pastor at the time of the alleged neglect. Authorities are continuing their investigation into the matter. The charges represent serious allegations against someone in a position of trust and authority in the community.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County 2026 election candidates finalized after qualifying period
cards.teaser: The candidate lineup for St. Lucie County's 2026 elections is now complete following the close of the qualifying period.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County's 2026 election candidates are now set after the qualifying period ended Friday. The final list of candidates who will appear on the ballot for various county races has been established. Voters will see these candidates compete in upcoming elections this year.

The qualifying period determined which candidates met the requirements to run for county offices. The election will allow St. Lucie County residents to choose their local representatives for the next term. Specific races and candidate names were included in the final qualifying roster released by election officials.

cards.headline: Three juveniles arrested after Fort Pierce shooting leaves teen critically injured
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce police arrested three juveniles Thursday night after a shooting on Avenue N left a 16-year-old in critical condition.
cards.body:
Three juveniles were arrested Thursday night in Fort Pierce after detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N. The detectives saw three juveniles fleeing in different directions and discovered another juvenile laying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter and apprehended the three suspects. One was caught by a sheriff's office K9 and another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old victim remained in critical condition Friday morning. One of the arrested juveniles, a 16-year-old, faces charges of attempted homicide, tampering with evidence and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie teen becomes first from St. Lucie County named Southeast Youth of the Year
hero.teaser: Enrique Rosario Liz, valedictorian at Port St. Lucie High School, made history as the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to earn the regional title and will compete nationally in October.
hero.body:
Enrique Rosario Liz has achieved a historic milestone as the first member of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County to receive the Southeast Region Youth of the Year award. The Port St. Lucie High School valedictorian will now travel to New York City on October 1 to compete for the national title. The Southeast Region Youth of the Year award honors outstanding teenagers who demonstrate strong academics, solid values, and a commitment to serving their communities.

Enrique's path to this recognition spans eight years. He arrived in the United States from the Dominican Republic as an 8-year-old who did not speak English. With support from his school and the local Boys & Girls Club, he transformed himself into a capable student and leader. Reflecting on his achievement, Enrique said, "I could never have imagined this moment when I was 8 years old. It's a privilege to share my journey, and I hope it inspires belief in every young person who needs a helping hand and an opportunity." His rise from newcomer to valedictorian demonstrates his determination and work ethic. This fall, he will enroll at the University of Florida.

Will Armstead, CEO of Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County, highlighted Enrique's character and resilience. "Enrique's achievement is historic, but his character impresses me most. He's turned challenges into opportunities and advocated for others, all with humility and determination," Armstead said. Travis Leonard, owner of A&G Concrete Pools and a longtime Youth of the Year judge, also praised the teenager's performance. "From the start, Enrique stood out. Thanks to his hard work and all those who support him, we finally have a Southeast Region Youth of the Year. I believe he's ready for the national competition, and I'm proud of him and our whole community," Leonard said.

Enrique's parents expressed gratitude for the opportunities their son received. "We're grateful to God for every opportunity and to Boys & Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County for helping Enrique grow as a leader and a person," they said. The Youth of the Year program represents Boys & Girls Clubs of America's highest recognition for teenagers who serve as role models and change-makers in their communities. As Enrique prepares for the national stage, his accomplishments continue to inspire young people throughout St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: Vero Beach man charged with killing grandmother who welcomed him into her home
cards.teaser: Nicholas Leonard Ivey, 29, faces murder charges in the death of his 76-year-old grandmother Patricia Ann DiBella, who was found dead at her home on Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach in February.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Friday that 29-year-old Nicholas Leonard Ivey now faces charges of murder and tampering with physical evidence in the death of his 76-year-old grandmother, Patricia Ann DiBella. According to investigators, Ivey admitted to killing DiBella, who had opened her home to him at 5090 Fairways Circle north of Vero Beach. A welfare check requested by family members on February 2 led deputies to discover DiBella's body inside her residence, where Ivey was taken into custody at the scene. Since February, Ivey has been held at the Indian River County Jail on related charges before being formally charged with murder on June 3. He is being held without bond.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a statement that no one should lose their life at the hands of someone they trusted and welcomed into their home. The sheriff's office reminded the community that domestic violence can take many forms and can affect anyone. Anyone experiencing domestic violence or in danger is urged to call 911, SafeSpace at 772-288-7023, or the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233.

cards.headline: Orlando Health provides health screenings to Indian River County employees
cards.teaser: Orlando Health conducted health screenings for Indian River County government employees, providing wellness services to local workers.
cards.body:
Orlando Health offered health screenings to Indian River County employees on Friday, according to Hometown News Treasure Coast. The screenings provided county workers access to wellness evaluations and health assessments.

The health screening program brought medical services directly to county employees, allowing them to receive preventive care and health information during the workday. The initiative represents a partnership between Orlando Health and the county government to support employee wellness.

cards.headline: Indian River County faces $50 million budget loss under property tax amendment
cards.teaser: Indian River County could lose approximately $50 million from its $597 million budget if voters approve a property tax amendment on the November ballot.
cards.body:
Indian River County leaders gathered Friday morning at the Heritage Center in Vero Beach to discuss a property tax amendment appearing on the November ballot. The amendment would raise the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. According to the Tax Payers Association, the county's $597 million budget could lose approximately $50 million in funding by 2028. Laura Moss, vice chair of the Indian River County Commission, criticized the measure as state interference in local governance. Lance Lunceford, president of the Indian River County Tax Payers Association, called it an unsound, unplanned piece of public policy.

Fire rescue services face particularly significant cuts. Christen Brewer, president of Indian River Firefighters, said the department could lose $15 to $20 million of its $70 million budget, with 79.1 percent of funding coming from ad valorem taxes. Three projected fire stations may not be built if the budget shortfall occurs. Lunceford warned the amendment represents a tax shift rather than a tax cut, likely requiring the county to raise taxes on non-homesteaded and commercial properties and increase costs for services such as impact fees and utility fees to compensate for lost revenue.

cards.headline: Delray Beach struggles to replace Pride memorial amid state restrictions
cards.teaser: Ten years after the Pulse nightclub massacre, Delray Beach residents face mounting obstacles to creating a new memorial after the state removed a rainbow-painted intersection that honored the 49 victims.
cards.body:
A rainbow-painted Pride intersection in Delray Beach was sandblasted away by the Florida Department of Transportation in August 2025, removing a mural that local residents had created and funded themselves to honor Pulse nightclub massacre victims. The state removal was part of a statewide push to regulate road markings and eliminate political and ideological messaging from roads. Similar crosswalks were removed in Orlando, including one outside the Pulse nightclub itself, while Boynton Beach preemptively took down its Pride crosswalk and West Palm Beach removed one in Northwood before later installing a rainbow corner in a nearby park. Delray Beach initially considered legal action but abandoned the idea due to potential costs.

Local advocate Ronnie Dunayer and other residents formed the Delray Beach Pride Memorial Committee and designed a rainbow pyramid monument to honor Pulse victims, proposing Old School Square near the Eagle Scout monument as the location. However, Senate Bill 1134, which passed 25-11 in the Senate and 77-37 in the House and awaits the governor's decision, would ban local governments from funding or supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Commissioner Juli Casal stated that private funding and private property could allow the project to proceed without city involvement. Dunayer is reaching out to state leaders and national organizations to find solutions.

cards.headline: Daughter files wrongful death suit after fatal Florida Turnpike crash in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Angeline Dowdian filed a lawsuit against the truck driver, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson after her mother Faniola Joseph died in an August 2025 crash on the Florida Turnpike.
cards.body:
On August 12, 2025, Herby Dufresne, 30, Faniola Joseph, 37, and Rodrigue Dor, 54, died when their minivan became wedged underneath a semi-truck in St. Lucie County. The truck driver, Harjinder Singh, worked for White Hawk Carriers and allegedly attempted an illegal U-turn in a clearly marked "No U-turn" zone. Joseph had been living in Indiana and had come south to purchase goods to resell in her shop.

Angeline Dowdian, Joseph's 22-year-old daughter, filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Singh, White Hawk Carriers, and freight broker C.H. Robinson, alleging negligence and unsafe practices. Represented by attorney Dax Bello of Stuart law firm Tillman, Fox, Bianchi & Kane, and co-counsel Mark Brumer of Brumer & Brumer, the lawsuit argues that C.H. Robinson knowingly gave business to White Hawk Carriers despite serious safety violations. Bello cited a May 14 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribbean Transport, which clarified that federal law does not shield freight brokers from state negligence claims when unsafe drivers are placed on the road. Singh faces criminal traffic homicide charges in Florida, and White Hawk Carriers has since shut down.

cards.headline: 16-year-old charged with attempted homicide after Fort Pierce shooting leaves teen in critical condition
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old suspect was arrested and charged after another 16-year-old was shot Thursday night on Avenue N in Fort Pierce and remains in critical condition.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old has been charged with attempted homicide following a shooting Thursday night in Fort Pierce. According to Fort Pierce police, detectives from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office heard gunshots while traveling on Avenue N and observed three juveniles fleeing in different directions. Officers discovered another juvenile lying on the sidewalk on top of a bike with gunshot wounds. The victim remained in critical condition at a local hospital as of Friday morning.

Detectives and officers established a perimeter in the area and apprehended all three suspects. One was captured by a sheriff's office K9, while another was found hiding in a recycling container. Two weapons were recovered at the scene. The 16-year-old suspect was charged with attempted homicide, tampering with evidence, and unlawful carry of a firearm by a person under 18. He was taken to the Department of Juvenile Justice.
